title: Designing Digital Health Systems Around Real-World Needs
author: The Lattice
excerpt: A useful digital health platform starts with the people, workflows and care settings it is meant to support. Explore a human-centred approach to healthcare technology design.
content:
Technology Should Fit the Realities of Care

Healthcare teams work across busy clinics, hospitals, laboratories and community settings. A digital tool is valuable when it supports the way people actually deliver care, rather than adding another layer of complexity.

Start with Discovery

Needs assessment, workflow observation and conversations with users help uncover the real problem. This early work can reveal where information is lost, where processes slow down and where a carefully designed digital intervention could make a difference.

Design, Test and Improve

Rapid prototypes allow clinicians, administrators and other stakeholders to respond to a solution before it is fully built. Iterative testing helps teams refine usability, information flows and operational fit.

From Idea to Implementation

The Lattice brings together technology, product thinking and practical problem-solving to explore digital solutions for complex environments. This sample article illustrates a possible editorial direction.

title: Interoperability: Connecting Healthcare Data for Better Decisions
author: The Lattice
excerpt: When health systems can exchange information consistently, care teams and public health programmes gain a clearer picture. Learn why interoperability matters.
content:
The Challenge of Fragmented Information

Healthcare information is often spread across facilities, applications and administrative systems. When these systems cannot communicate, staff may need to enter the same information repeatedly and decision-makers may struggle to build a complete view.

Why Standards Matter

Standards such as HL7 FHIR provide shared structures and conventions for representing and exchanging health information. Terminologies such as SNOMED CT and ICD help systems describe clinical concepts consistently.

Interoperability Is More Than an Interface

Successful exchange depends on governance, data quality, privacy, security and the workflows around the technology. Teams need to agree what information is shared, who can access it and how it will be used.

Building Connected Systems

Connected systems can help organisations reduce information silos and support more informed decisions across healthcare environments.

title: From Connected Medical Devices to Actionable Information
author: The Lattice
excerpt: Medical devices can generate valuable data, but that information needs reliable connectivity and thoughtful workflows to become useful to healthcare teams.
content:
Making Device Data Useful

Patient monitors, diagnostic equipment and point-of-care devices can produce information that supports clinical and operational workflows. The challenge is ensuring that data moves reliably from the device to the people and systems that need it.

Choosing the Right Connection

Depending on the device and setting, integration may involve Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or other communication technologies. The right approach depends on range, reliability, security, power requirements and the environment in which the device is used.

Designing the Complete Workflow

Device integration should account for pairing, identity, data validation, exception handling and what happens when connectivity is interrupted. A successful solution considers the full journey, not just the transfer of data.

Hardware and Software Together

Connected products work best when hardware, software and user workflows are considered as one integrated experience.

title: AI-Enabled Health Platforms: Supporting Experts, Not Replacing Them
author: The Lattice
excerpt: Thoughtfully designed AI can help organise information, identify patterns and support decision-making while keeping people and accountability at the centre.
content:
Useful AI Begins with a Clear Problem

AI is most meaningful when it addresses a defined workflow or information challenge. In healthcare, that may include organising large volumes of data, classifying content or helping specialists recognise patterns that deserve closer attention.

Fit the Model to the Workflow

A platform should reflect the language, data and decisions of its intended users. It also needs clear ways to review outputs, handle uncertainty and escalate cases that require human judgement.

Trust Requires Responsible Design

Privacy, security, transparency and ongoing evaluation should be considered from the beginning. Teams should understand what data is used, what the system can and cannot do, and how performance is monitored.

Human-Centred Intelligence

The goal of AI-enabled systems should be to make complex work more manageable while preserving expert oversight and meaningful human decisions.

title: Designing Digital Tools for Primary and Community Healthcare
author: The Lattice
excerpt: Primary care platforms need to support frontline teams, continuity of care and programme visibility across facilities and communities.
content:
Care Begins Close to the Community

Primary and community healthcare teams often coordinate multiple services with limited time and resources. Digital tools can help organise registrations, follow-ups, referrals and programme information when they are designed around frontline realities.

Keep Workflows Practical

Interfaces should make common tasks clear, reduce duplicate entry and work across the devices available to staff. Training, support and sensible defaults are as important as the software itself.

Build for Continuity

Useful platforms connect information across visits and levels of care. Open standards and carefully designed data exchange can help different parts of a health system work together.

Scale with Purpose

Digital public health systems should be designed to support real service delivery, interoperability and the needs of large health programmes.

title: Privacy and Security by Design in Digital Health
author: The Lattice
excerpt: Protecting sensitive information is not a final checklist. Privacy and security need to shape the architecture, access controls and everyday operation of a digital health system.
content:
Build Trust into the System

Digital health platforms may handle personal, clinical and operational information. Protecting that information is essential to user trust and responsible service delivery.

Plan Security from the Start

Good design considers identity and access management, least-privilege permissions, secure data transfer, audit trails, backups and incident response. These decisions are more effective when they are part of the initial architecture.

Privacy Is Also a Workflow Question

Teams should define why information is collected, who needs to see it, how long it is retained and when it can be shared. Clear governance helps translate privacy principles into daily practice.

Responsible Digital Innovation

Security and privacy should be considered throughout the lifecycle of a digital product, from initial planning to implementation and ongoing maintenance.
